# The Map {.unnumbered}

This book makes one argument in twelve chapters, and it helps to see the whole of it before
starting. Three pictures carry it: the space in which every learning problem and every method sits,
the lineage that connects the methods, and the handful of independent choices that every method name
hides.

## The space: what the feedback says, and who generated the data

Supervised learning and reinforcement learning are not two kinds of machine learning. They are
regions of one space ([What Makes a Problem RL](01-what-makes-a-problem-rl.qmd)). Along one axis, the
feedback is *instructive* (a label says what the right answer was) or *evaluative* (a reward says
only how good the given answer was), with comparisons and teacher signals in between. Along the
other, the data is a *fixed* dataset or is *generated by the learner's own policy*. A third axis,
not shown as a position, is whether credit arrives immediately or must be assigned across a
sequence of actions.

![Every method in the book placed by the kind of feedback it learns from (vertical) and by who generated its training data (horizontal); marker shape shows whether credit is assigned per sequence or per token. Supervised fine-tuning and off-policy distillation sit in the instructive, fixed-data corner; the policy-gradient family sits in the evaluative, self-generated corner; offline preference methods sit between. Positions are read from the same records that generate the unified table.](../images/feedback_space.png){#fig-feedback-space}

## The lineage: one tree, a few branches

Almost every named method modifies an earlier one, usually in exactly one respect. The tree grows
from two main roots, the policy gradient (REINFORCE) and behavior cloning (SFT). From REINFORCE come
PPO and PPO-based RLHF, which branches into the direct preference methods and GRPO's line of
critic-free policy gradients; the other critic-free methods (RLOO, ReMax) and the calibration reward
modify REINFORCE directly. Filtered imitation and distillation grow from SFT. Two methods stand
alone: best-of-$n$ sampling, which modifies no training method, and TypeSafe's RLCD, whose lineage is
undisclosed.

![The method lineage: each arrow points from a method to the one that modifies it, laid out by generation (the length of the chain of modifications from a root) and colored by family, with the year of each method's primary source (SFT and best-of-$n$, which have no single primary source, carry none). Generated with networkx from the same records as the unified table.](../images/method_lineage.png){#fig-method-lineage}

Each node links to a chapter:

| Family | Methods | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| classical RL | REINFORCE, PPO | [Policy Gradients](02-policy-gradients.qmd), [Keeping Updates Stable](03-keeping-updates-stable.qmd) |
| the hub | the KL-regularized objective, $\pi^\star$, PPO-based RLHF | [The Shared Target, and RLHF with PPO](06-the-shared-target.qmd) |
| direct preference | DPO, online DPO, IPO, KTO, SimPO, ORPO | [Direct Preference Methods](07-direct-preference-methods.qmd) |
| critic-free policy gradients | RLOO, ReMax, GRPO, Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GSPO, CISPO | [Policy Gradients Without a Critic](08-policy-gradients-without-a-critic.qmd) |
| imitation and distillation | SFT, best-of-$n$, rejection-sampling fine-tuning, STaR, ReST, RAFT, off- and on-policy distillation | [Learning by Imitating a Better Distribution](09-imitating-a-better-distribution.qmd) |
| calibration rewards | correctness + proper scoring rule; RLCD | [Rewarding Calibration](10-rewarding-calibration.qmd) |
| where it is heading | multi-turn and agentic RL | [What RL Actually Does to a Model](11-what-rl-does-to-a-model.qmd) |

## The axes a method name hides

A method name bundles several independent choices. The book unbundles them into the same fields for
every method, its *method card*, and the [unified table](../unified-table.qmd) lines them up.

| Axis | The choices | Where it is derived |
|---|---|---|
| **Signal source** | demonstrations · pairwise preferences · binary desirability · learned scalar reward · verifiable reward · AI or judge feedback · teacher log-probabilities · a scored probability | [rewards](05-rewards.qmd), [calibration](10-rewarding-calibration.qmd) |
| **Data regime** ($q$) | offline · on-policy · slightly off-policy (batch reuse) · iterated | [what makes a problem RL](01-what-makes-a-problem-rl.qmd), [stable updates](03-keeping-updates-stable.qmd) |
| **Estimator and weight** ($w$) | maximum likelihood · pairwise logistic likelihood · policy gradient with no baseline, a critic, leave-one-out, or group mean and std | [policy gradients](02-policy-gradients.qmd), [critic-free](08-policy-gradients-without-a-critic.qmd) |
| **Stability** | KL in the reward · KL in the loss · clip / trust region · reference-free · entropy bonus | [stable updates](03-keeping-updates-stable.qmd) |
| **Credit granularity** | sequence · token · step (process rewards) | [the LLM as a policy](04-the-llm-as-a-policy.qmd) |
| **Models in memory** | policy · reference · reward model · critic · teacher | [the shared target](06-the-shared-target.qmd) |

## Reading paths

Front to back is the intended order: each part makes the next one feel inevitable. Three shorter paths
also work. If you know classical RL and want the LLM-specific part, start at
[The LLM as a Policy](04-the-llm-as-a-policy.qmd). If you want the single idea that unifies the methods,
read [Policy Gradients](02-policy-gradients.qmd) and then
[The Shared Target](06-the-shared-target.qmd). If you have a new paper in hand, go to the five-minute
recipe in the [decision guide](12-decision-guide.qmd).
